sentences.text: The species is named Achelousaurus horneri, and it was a large centrosaurine dinosaur estimated to be about 6 meters long and weigh 3 metric tons.
Adult individuals possess nasal bosses that are relatively small, thin, and heavily covered with pits.
Adult Achelousaurus skulls featured a rough, heavily pitted boss on the snout instead of a horn found in many other ceratopsids.
The neck shield of Achelousaurus featured two prominent large spikes that pointed backward and curved outward to the sides.
If specimen MOR 591 belongs to Achelousaurus, the genus may have reached adult size faster than Einiosaurus, as it was the same size as a larger Einiosaurus skull but younger.
The genus Achelousaurus was described by Scott D. Sampson in 1994, following the collection of the first fossils in Montana in 1987.
All known specimens of Achelousaurus were recovered from the Two Medicine Formation in Glacier County, Montana.
The informal name "Styracosaurus makeli" appeared in a book by Stephen Czerkas in 1990 as an invalid nomen nudum.
As a ceratopsian, Achelousaurus was a herbivore with a high metabolic rate.
A 2013 study determined that Achelousaurus was restricted to feeding on vegetation no higher than 1 meter.
Paleontologists proposed that the rough bosses of Achelousaurus were covered by thick pads of keratinized skin, similar to the bosses of modern muskoxen.
Research in 2009 suggested Achelousaurus used its nasal and supraorbital bosses for butting or ramming rivals during combat.
Researcher Dodson concluded that monospecific Achelousaurus bone beds confirm these dinosaurs lived in herds.
Oxygen isotope analysis of Achelousaurus bones suggests they were homeothermic endotherms.
Achelousaurus belongs to the clade Pachyrostra, meaning "thick-snouts", within the Ceratopsia, and lived during the Campanian age as a member of the Centrosaurinae subgroup of ceratopsians.
In 1995, Sampson formally classified Achelousaurus within the Ceratopsidae family, specifically the Centrosaurinae subfamily.
All phylogenetic analyses identify Achelousaurus and Pachyrhinosaurus as sister groups.

Achelousaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 77 to 74.8 million years ago, and also lived between 83 and 74 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
These animals lived on a narrow coastal strip on the east coast of Laramidia, bordered by the Western Interior Seaway and the 3 to 4 km high proto-Rocky Mountains.
Achelousaurus lived during the phase when the coastal habitat was at its narrowest, experiencing the strongest selection pressures.
Horner proposed that the succession of fossils represented anagenesis, where later forms were simply evolved versions of earlier ones rather than distinct species.
In 1995, Sampson revised the timeline, estimating 860,000 years passed after the Brachyceratops quarry and 640,000 years after the Einiosaurus beds, contradicting Horner's shorter timeframe.

Wilson and colleagues attributed the differences between Einiosaurus and Achelousaurus to heterochrony, or differential development speeds of traits during an individual's lifetime, and in 2020 found Stellasaurus intermediate between Styracosaurus and Einiosaurus in morphology and stratigraphy, supporting its role in an anagenetic lineage.
The reduced habitat size caused a population bottleneck, which Horner suggested made rapid evolution possible.
Scientists debate whether Styracosaurus albertensis or Einiosaurus was the direct ancestor of Achelousaurus.
